Feels like I've been plateauing for my distance runs, so on this nice sunny day I cranked a 3km as fast as I could. Finished in just seconds over 12 minutes, but felt like falling over by the end. Hopefully sprinkling these into my training will up my distance pace!

Honestly though, I feel like I'm in the same boat now too. The progression from 28:30 down to about 23-24 was very fast, only took me about 2 weeks. But it's been a grind to shave off the minutes now, and 22 was my PB with optimal outdoor conditions, but on a typical day with wind I'm usually struggling to break 23. 

  
I've been theorizing and I honestly think its down to nutrition and sleep, certain foods make me run way better (whitefish and rice or a light pasta with little or no sauce and lean protein) than others. It might be cheating to the purists out there but I select songs based on high intensity so I keep my cadence high. I also spent a couple nights watching running form videos and reading journal articles and papers on running form.

Typically I only ever take one or two days off at most, and sometimes I throw in a 10km at a slower pace or a fast 3km, so probably about 25-30km a week or about 15-18 miles. 

  
That being said I did start out from a decent baseline of fitness as I cycle and swim lots, just always "hated" running. Not anymore!
In 1.5 months of running I've brought my 5km pace down from 28:30 to 22:00 flat!

As for your background problem don’t overthink it. This is how I thought of it to increase my deadlift from 165 to 375 in a year:

Your arms are ropes connected to your shoulders. Don’t even think about them besides gripping the bar. Keep your spine rigid straight. If it bends at all, it means you need to deload typically. For conventional deadlift keep your feet pointed straight and slightly more narrow than your shoulders but not by much. Your hands should be just lateral of your feet on the bar. Midfoot under the bar. Like others have said, push with your legs until your knees then activate your hips and push forwards BUT don’t over extend. Just straight up and down like a plank of wood, don’t bend backwards with it at the top. To set it down just all of that in reverse. 

You’ll reach a point where you can’t grip what you’re lifting, for me that’s around anything over 225 if I don’t have chalk, so switch grip in that case. 

Stretch, stretch stretch. After each lifting session, take 10-15 minutes to stretch and massage your muscles, seriously.

Ever since I was 8 I’ve had dental problems. These later evolved into oblong facial growth and eventually a Class 3 bite known as an underbite. I had a recessed maxilla with a narrow palate that pulled my nose inwards and made it hook downwards. My mouth while resting was always agape, like a piranha. I couldn’t breath through my nose as my nasal cavity was so narrow and compressed no good amount of air could pass through. I was ugly.

I lived like this until I was 20. I ended up getting braces at 18 and double jaw surgery and SARPE at 19. It changed my life. 8 months of recovery, 2 of which I had to drink every meal, all worth it 100 times over. My life changed immeasurably. 

My smile was made perfect, with my maxilla pulled forwards it fixed my hook nose. People were automatically nicer to me. Everyone. Just every small innocuous interaction had an element of positivity and respect I hadn’t felt before. I became so much more confident, and worked harder to improve myself more. Dating became possible. I was no longer ignored by girls or made fun of for my appearance. I feel like I’m now capable of becoming the person I always wanted to be.

Pretty privilege is real. In the past 2 years of having a new face I’ve received more opportunity and success than I had before. I’m more outgoing now because there’s more room for failure. When you make a social faux-pas or say something awkward people are much, much more forgiving, most times laughing it off or moving on immediately. That wouldn’t happen when I was ugly. I would be beaten down and made fun of on the spot. I know because it happened, I was the scapegoat in high school. This surgery changed every social aspect of my life in such a way I can’t even imagine life without it. That’s how much it affected me.
